passages.t: Who has believed? The despised man of sorrows
passages.happening:
A group of speakers now takes up the song. ‘Who has believed our message? And to whom has the arm of the LORD been revealed?’ (verse 1).

They remember how the Servant looked. ‘He grew up before Him like a tender shoot, and like a root out of dry ground’ (verse 2). There was nothing about him to draw anyone. ‘He had no stately form or majesty to attract us, no beauty that we should desire Him’ (verse 2).

‘He was despised and rejected by men, a man of sorrows, acquainted with grief’ (verse 3). He was like someone people turn their faces away from. ‘He was despised, and we esteemed Him not’ (verse 3).
passages.hearers:
This is the heart of the fourth Servant Song, which began at 52:13. In the earlier songs the Servant was chosen to bring justice to the nations, called to restore Israel and be a light to the Gentiles, and beaten for his faithfulness while he trusted God. Now his suffering is explained.

The song falls into five stanzas of about three verses each. God speaks in the first and the last. In the three middle stanzas an unnamed group speaks. They never say who they are, and the song never names the Servant. Readers have found their own place among the speakers ever since.

The arm of the LORD, his strength in action, has been promised all through these chapters. Now it is revealed in a man no one would look at twice. A shoot from dry ground was a picture of small, unpromising life. The phrase acquainted with grief can also be read as known by sickness. In that world serious illness and disfigurement made people turn their faces away.
passages.later: John quotes verse 1 of those who saw Jesus' signs and still did not believe: “Lord, who has believed our message? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (John 12:38). Isaiah had promised ‘a shoot will spring up from the stump of Jesse’ (Isaiah 11:1).
passages.asks: The Servant had nothing in his appearance to draw anyone. Ask what you expect God's strength to look like, and whether you would have recognized it here. And ask whom you have looked away from because of how they looked.

passages.t: Pierced for transgressions, and all gone astray
passages.happening:
Then the speakers' confession. ‘Surely He took on our infirmities and carried our sorrows; yet we considered Him stricken by God, struck down and afflicted’ (verse 4).

‘But He was pierced for our transgressions, He was crushed for our iniquities; the punishment that brought us peace was upon Him, and by His stripes we are healed’ (verse 5).

‘We all like sheep have gone astray, each one has turned to his own way; and the LORD has laid upon Him the iniquity of us all’ (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
These three verses are the turning point of the song. They are built on a sharp contrast between he and the speakers. He took their infirmities, and they thought him struck by God. He was pierced for their transgressions, and they all went astray like sheep. The stanza begins and ends with the whole group, all of them in the guilt and all of them in the provision.

The speakers had assumed what the ancient world assumed: serious illness and disfigurement were signs of divine punishment. Job's friends argued exactly that. When the speakers saw the Servant diseased and struck down, they concluded God was punishing him. The shock of the song is that they were right that God was involved and wrong about why.

The word for stripes, or welts, is the word Isaiah used in his first chapter for Israel's beaten body, with wounds not bound up. Now the welts are on the Servant, and by them the many are healed.

The words for sin and for bearing it run through every stanza. Bearing iniquity can mean carrying its guilt, as the scapegoat carried the people's sins into the wilderness. When God bears iniquity, it means he forgives it. Here the Servant carries what is lifted from others.
passages.later: Peter writes of Jesus, ‘He Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree’ (1 Peter 2:24), and quotes verse 5 and verse 6 in the same breath. Matthew applies verse 4 to Jesus' healings: ‘He took on our infirmities and carried our diseases’ (Matthew 8:17).
passages.hard:
The speakers thought the Servant was sick and struck down because God was punishing him. Does the Bible teach that illness is a punishment?

The song says the speakers were wrong. They saw a man diseased and assumed he was guilty, and they learned that he carried what was theirs. Job's friends made the same mistake (Job 4:7), and when the disciples asked Jesus whose sin had made a man blind, he answered, ‘Neither this man nor his parents sinned’ (John 9:3). The song gives no one a warrant to look at a sick or disabled person and assume a hidden sin.

It needs to be said plainly. The Bible does not teach that sickness comes from too little faith, or that a person who stays ill did not believe enough. Paul prayed and was not healed, and no one blames him. If you live with chronic illness, pain or disability, you are not a failure of faith. Your worth to God does not rise or fall with your body. If the weight of it is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a doctor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The speakers misread suffering, and the truth undid them. Ask whose suffering you have misread as deserved. And ask what it would mean to say verse 6 about yourself, that you too have turned to your own way.

passages.t: Silent like a lamb, and a grave with the wicked
passages.happening:
‘He was oppressed and afflicted, yet He did not open His mouth’ (verse 7). ‘He was led like a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is silent, so He did not open His mouth’ (verse 7).

‘By oppression and judgment He was taken away, and who can recount His descendants?’ (verse 8). He was cut off from the land of the living. ‘He was stricken for the transgression of My people’ (verse 8).

‘He was assigned a grave with the wicked, and with a rich man in His death, although He had done no violence, nor was any deceit in His mouth’ (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
The lamb led to slaughter and the sheep before its shearers came from the farm life of Judah's hill country, where animals went to death and to shearing without protest. Jeremiah used the same picture of himself when men plotted to kill him.

Verse 8 calls what was done to the Servant oppression and judgment. It was a trial, and it was unjust. He was cut off from the land of the living, the Bible's way of saying he died.

Burial mattered deeply in Israel. To lie in the family tomb was to be gathered to one's fathers, and to be denied it was a final disgrace. The law required that an executed criminal be buried the same day. The rich of Jerusalem carved fine tombs from the rock. Verse 9 holds both: a grave among the wicked, and a rich man in his death.

Whether the Servant actually dies is debated. Most readers, Jewish and Christian, take verses 8 and 9 as death followed by vindication beyond it. Some argue the language of death is a picture of extreme suffering from which he was rescued.
passages.later: An Ethiopian official was reading verses 7 and 8 when Philip met him, and Philip ‘began with this very Scripture and told him the good news about Jesus’ (Acts 8:35). Peter writes that Christ ‘committed no sin, and no deceit was found in His mouth’ (1 Peter 2:22), the words of verse 9.
passages.hard:
Who is the Servant: Israel, the prophet, or the Messiah Jesus?

The Ethiopian's question is still the first one: ‘who is the prophet talking about, himself or someone else?’ (Acts 8:34). Isaiah often names Israel as God's servant (41:8; 44:1-2; 49:3). On this reading, held by the medieval Jewish commentators Rashi, Ibn Ezra and David Kimhi and by most Jewish interpreters today, the Servant is the people of Israel, humiliated and scattered among the nations, and the speakers are the nations and their kings (52:15), who at last see that Israel suffered unjustly and that its suffering served their good. Others limit the Servant to a faithful remnant. Others see an individual of the prophet's own day: the prophet himself, or a figure like Jeremiah, whose own words of a lamb led to slaughter are close to this song (Jeremiah 11:19). Critical scholars, Jewish and Christian, add that reading the song as a detailed forecast of Jesus lifts it out of its setting in the exile.

Christian interpreters answer that the Servant here cannot simply be the nation. In 49:5-6 he has a mission to restore Israel. He suffers without sin (verse 9), while the nation in these chapters suffers for its sins (40:2). His suffering is willing and for others, for the transgression of God's people (verse 8). Many Christians hold that the collective and individual readings belong together: the Servant is Israel as God meant it to be, one person who does for Israel and the nations what the nation could not. The New Testament names that person as Jesus (Acts 8:35; 1 Peter 2:21-25). Ancient Jewish tradition also read the song of the Messiah in places, though not as a dying Messiah who atones.

This is where Jews and Christians most sharply part, and each answer is tied to what each confesses about the Messiah. The song gives no one a warrant for contempt toward the Jewish people.
passages.asks: The Servant did not open his mouth to defend himself. Ask what it would cost you to keep silent when you are wronged, and when silence would be wrong. And ask how you answer the Ethiopian's question for yourself.

passages.t: The LORD's will, a guilt offering, and the light of life
passages.happening:
‘Yet it was the LORD’s will to crush Him and to cause Him to suffer’ (verse 10). When his soul is made a guilt offering, he will see his offspring and prolong his days, and the good pleasure of the LORD will prosper in his hand (verse 10).

‘After the anguish of His soul, He will see the light of life and be satisfied’ (verse 11). ‘By His knowledge My righteous Servant will justify many, and He will bear their iniquities’ (verse 11).

God will give him a portion with the great, and he will divide the spoils with the strong, ‘because He has poured out His life unto death, and He was numbered with the transgressors’ (verse 12). ‘Yet He bore the sin of many and made intercession for the transgressors’ (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
God speaks again, as he did at the start. The song ends where it began, with the Servant exalted, but now the reader knows the cost.

The guilt offering, asham, was the sacrifice brought to make amends for a wrong, especially a wrong against what belonged to God, with restitution added. Every Israelite knew it. The Servant's life itself becomes that offering.

The Great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran, copied around 125 BC, contains this chapter essentially as Bibles have it. Its most important difference is in verse 11, where it reads that he will see light, a reading other ancient copies share and the BSB follows with the light of life. Life after death is in view: the one cut off from the land of the living sees offspring and prolongs his days.

The word many returns again and again. He justifies many, bears the sin of many, and the many kings of 52:15 are silenced. The one is set against the many all through the song.
passages.later: On the night before his death Jesus quoted verse 12, ‘He was numbered with the transgressors’, and said it ‘must be fulfilled in Me’ (Luke 22:37). Hebrews says ‘Christ was offered once to bear the sins of many’ (Hebrews 9:28).
passages.hard:
How can it be just for one person's suffering to take away another's sin? And does this teach that suffering under another's hand is good?

The objection is serious, and the prophets themselves raise its ground: each person bears his own guilt (Ezekiel 18:20). The sixteenth-century writer Faustus Socinus argued that guilt cannot be moved from one person to another and that punishing the innocent for the guilty is unjust. In 1989 the theologians Joanne Carlson Brown and Rebecca Parker argued that doctrines of redemptive suffering picture God as an abusive father and teach victims to accept abuse. Jewish interpreters add that the Hebrew Bible nowhere else makes a human life a sacrifice for sin.

The answers begin in the song itself. The Servant is not a third party seized against his will. He pours out his life (verse 12), goes willingly (verse 7), and intercedes for the transgressors. The song calls the human process that killed him oppression and injustice (verse 8), even while it says the LORD's purpose stood behind it (verse 10). Christian writers such as John Stott answered the charge of injustice by saying that God does not punish a reluctant third party but gives himself in the person of his Son. The church confesses ‘that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures’ (1 Corinthians 15:3). How best to explain that for is a question on which faithful Christians still differ.

The cross gives no warrant for anyone to hurt another person, and it does not ask anyone to stay where they are being harmed. The Servant's suffering was his own to give. It was never taken from him by a husband, a parent or a pastor in God's name.

If someone is hurting you, at home, at work or in a church, your safety comes first. Tell someone you trust and get help; the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The Servant bore the sin of many and prayed for the transgressors. Ask whether you believe your own sin was among what he carried. And ask whom you would find it hardest to pray for, as he prayed for those who put him among the transgressors.
